61: Hill continues the deeply personal story of his son Blair, born without ears. He knew his son would hear and speak—how, he wasn't sure, but he would find a way. He quoted Emerson: 'The whole course of things goes to teach us faith. We need only obey. There is guidance for each of us, and by lowly listening, we shall hear the right word.' The right word was DESIRE. Hill never receded from his desire that his son not be deaf and mute. He recalled his own written principle: 'Our only limitations are those we set up in our own minds,' and for the first time wondered if it were true, given this limitation the child hadn't set up. He resolved to transplant into the child's mind his own BURNING DESIRE for ways to convey sound to his brain without ears. As soon as the child was old enough, Hill would fill his mind so completely with a BURNING DESIRE to hear that Nature would translate it into physical reality. He spoke to no one about this. Every day he renewed his pledge. As the child grew, they observed slight hearing. When the child reached talking age, he made no attempt to speak, but responded to certain sounds. That was all Hill needed. Then a breakthrough: they bought a Victrola phonograph, and the child went into ecstasies over music, playing one record—'It's a Long Way to Tipperary'—over and over for almost two hours with his teeth clamped on the edge of the case.
62: Hill explains the significance of the child clamping his teeth on the Victrola case wasn't clear until years later, when they learned about 'bone conduction' of sound. Hill discovered he could be heard clearly when speaking with his lips touching the child's mastoid bone. These discoveries gave him the means to translate his BURNING DESIRE into reality. He began transferring to the child's mind the desire to hear and speak, using bedtime stories designed to develop self-reliance, imagination, and a keen desire to hear. One story was emphasized with new dramatic coloring each time, designed to plant the thought that his disability was not a liability but an asset of great value. Hill acknowledges that despite his philosophy that EVERY ADVERSITY BRINGS WITH IT THE SEED OF AN EQUIVALENT ADVANTAGE, he had no idea how this affliction could become an asset. He continued wrapping that philosophy in bedtime stories anyway, hoping the child would eventually find a plan. Reason told him there was no adequate compensation for lack of ears, but DESIRE backed by FAITH pushed reason aside. In retrospect, Hill recognizes his son's faith in him was crucial—the child never questioned anything told him. Hill sold him the idea that he had a distinct advantage over his older brother.
63: The child's hearing gradually improved, and he showed no self-consciousness about his affliction. At age seven, the first evidence of Hill's method appeared: the child begged for months to sell newspapers, but his mother refused, fearing his deafness made streets unsafe. He took matters into his own hands—climbing through a kitchen window, borrowing six cents from a neighborhood shoemaker, investing in papers, selling out, reinvesting, and repeating until late evening. After paying back the six cents, he had a net profit of 42 cents. His mother found him asleep with money clenched in his hand—she cried, seeing a deaf boy risking his life. Hill laughed heartily, knowing his effort to plant self-faith had succeeded. He saw a brave, ambitious, self-reliant businessman whose stock in himself increased 100 percent through independent initiative. This resourcefulness pattern continued: when his older brother wanted something, he'd lie on the floor kicking and crying; when Blair wanted something, he'd plan a way to earn the money and buy it. Hill concludes his son taught him that disabilities can be converted into steppingstones unless accepted as obstacles and used as alibis. Blair went through grade school, high school, and college without hearing teachers except when they shouted at close range, never attending a special school.
64: Hill describes how they insisted Blair live as normal a life as possible, associating with hearing children, despite heated debates with school officials. In high school, a hearing aid was of no value. During his last week of college, the most important turning point occurred: through seeming chance, he received another hearing aid on trial. Reluctant after prior disappointment, he finally placed it on his head—and as if by magic, his lifelong DESIRE FOR NORMAL HEARING BECAME A REALITY. For the first time, he could hear practically as well as anyone with normal hearing. Overjoyed, he called his mother and heard her voice perfectly, heard his professors for the first time, heard the radio and movies, and could converse freely without people speaking loudly. Hill states they had refused to accept Nature's error and through PERSISTENT DESIRE induced Nature to correct it. But the victory wasn't complete—the boy still needed to convert his disability into an equivalent asset. Intoxicated with his new world of sound, he wrote an enthusiastic letter to the hearing aid manufacturer. Something in his letter—perhaps not written on the lines but behind them—caused the company to invite him to New York. While touring the factory and talking with the chief engineer about his Changed World, an inspiration flashed into his mind that would convert his affliction into an asset paying dividends in money and happiness to thousands.
65: The inspiration was to help millions of deaf people by sharing the story of his Changed World. He reached a decision to devote his life to serving the hard of hearing. He spent a month doing intensive research, analyzing the manufacturer's entire marketing system, figuring out ways to communicate with hearing-impaired people worldwide. He wrote a two-year plan and presented it to the company, which instantly gave him a position. He was destined to bring hope and practical relief to thousands who without his help would never have overcome their hearing disability. Hill was invited to attend a class the company conducted to teach deaf people to hear and speak. Skeptical but hopeful, he witnessed a demonstration showing the self-same principle he had used 20 years earlier with Blair. Hill states with certainty that Blair would have been unable to hear or speak if his mother and Hill hadn't shaped his mind. Dr. Irving Voorhees, a noted specialist, examined Blair and was astounded, saying 'theoretically, the boy should not be able to hear at all.' Hill reflects that when he planted DESIRE in Blair's mind, some strange influence caused Nature to become 'bridge-builder,' spanning the gulf of silence between his brain and the outer world by means medical specialists couldn't interpret.
66: Hill calls it sacrilege to pretend he fully understands how Nature performed this miracle, but considers it his duty to share what he knows. He believes nothing is impossible to the person who backs DESIRE with enduring FAITH. Blair's BURNING DESIRE for normal hearing was transmuted into reality. His disability, which could have sent a lesser person to the street with pencils and a tin cup, instead became the medium for rendering useful service to thousands and providing him employment at adequate compensation. Hill reflects that the 'white lie' he planted—leading Blair to BELIEVE his affliction would become a great asset—justified itself. He concludes: 'there is nothing, right or wrong, that BELIEF plus BURNING DESIRE cannot make real. These qualities are free to everyone.' In all his experience, Hill never handled a case more definitively demonstrating the power of DESIRE. He considers it providential that the experience came to someone prepared to serve as an example. He asks: if Mother Nature bends to the will of burning desire, can mere human beings defeat one? The mind uses every circumstance, individual, and physical thing as means of transmuting DESIRE into physical counterpart—perhaps science will one day uncover this secret.
67: Hill summarizes the method: three definite acts achieved the astounding result. First, he MIXED FAITH with the DESIRE for normal hearing and passed it to his son. Second, he communicated his desire in every conceivable way through persistent, continuous effort over years. Third, HE BELIEVED. Hill then shares the story of Mme. Schuman-Heink, whose death was recently reported. A short paragraph about her gives the clue to her success: early in her career, she visited the director of the Vienna Court Opera to audition. He refused after one look at the awkward, poorly dressed girl, exclaiming: 'With such a face, and with no personality at all, how can you ever expect to succeed in opera? My good child, give up the idea. Buy a sewing machine, and go to work. YOU CAN NEVER BE A SINGER.' Hill observes: 'Never is a long time!' The director knew singing technique but nothing about the power of desire when it becomes an obsession. Hill then tells of a business associate who became seriously ill and was hospitalized for surgery. The surgeon warned Hill there was little chance of seeing him alive again. But the patient whispered: 'Do not be disturbed, Chief, I will be out of here in a few days.' The nurse looked at Hill with pity, but the patient came through safely. The physician said: 'Nothing but his own desire to live saved him.'
68: Hill concludes Chapter 1 by affirming his belief in the power of DESIRE backed by FAITH, having seen it lift people from lowly beginnings to power and wealth, rob the grave of its victims, enable comebacks after defeat in a hundred ways, and provide his son with a normal, happy, successful life despite severe disability. He addresses those wounded by economic calamity—people who lost fortunes, positions, or must reorganize and stage comebacks—conveying that all achievement begins with an intense, BURNING DESIRE for something definite. Through 'mental chemistry' which Nature has never divulged, strong DESIRE recognizes no such word as 'impossible' and accepts no such reality as failure. Hill transitions to Chapter 2, noting Nature has given us the way to channel DESIRE unwaveringly toward goals: FAITH—The Second Step to Riches. The chapter ends with the statement: 'FAITH IS A STATE OF MIND WHICH MAY BE INDUCED BY AUTOSUGGESTION.'
69: This page opens Chapter 2: FAITH—Visualization and Belief in the Attainment of Desire (The Second Step to Riches). Hill defines FAITH as 'the head chemist of the mind'—when blended with the 'vibration of thought,' the subconscious mind picks up the vibration, translates it into its spiritual equivalent, and transmits it to Infinite Intelligence, as in prayer. He identifies FAITH, LOVE, and SEX as the most powerful positive emotions; when blended, they 'color' the vibration of thought so it instantly reaches the subconscious mind and is changed into its spiritual equivalent—the only form that induces a response from Infinite Intelligence. Love and faith are psychic/spiritual; sex is biological/physical. Their mixing opens a direct line between the finite human mind and Infinite Intelligence. Hill then introduces 'How to Develop Faith,' stating that FAITH is a state of mind which may be induced or created by affirmations or repeated instructions to the subconscious mind through autosuggestion. This is the key principle connecting Chapter 2 to Chapter 3 on autosuggestion.
70: Hill explains the method: by following instructions on autosuggestion (Chapter 3) and the subconscious mind (Chapter 11), one can CONVINCE the subconscious mind to believe in receiving what is asked for. The subconscious then acts on that belief, passing it back as FAITH followed by definite plans. He acknowledges the difficulty of describing how to develop faith where it doesn't exist—'almost as difficult as describing the color of red to a blind person.' However, faith is a state of mind developable at will after mastering the 13 principles, through voluntary application. The only method of voluntary development of faith is repetition or affirmation of orders to the subconscious mind. Hill illustrates with a criminologist's observation: 'When people first come into contact with crime, they abhor it. If they remain in contact for a time, they become accustomed to it and endure it. If they remain in contact long enough, they finally embrace it.' This demonstrates that any impulse of thought repeatedly passed to the subconscious is finally accepted and acted upon, being translated into its physical equivalent. Hill restates: ALL THOUGHTS WHICH HAVE BEEN EMOTIONALIZED (given feeling) AND MIXED WITH FAITH begin immediately to translate themselves into their physical equivalent.
